name: Resident Economic Empowerment and Sustainability (REES) for NYCHA Residents – NYCHA Development - Local Law 163
description: This dataset contains annual records from the Resident Economic Empowerment and Sustainability (REES) program, which serves New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) residents. Reported under Local Law 163, each row represents a NYCHA development in a given year from 2018 through 2024, with counts of residents served and average wages across several program categories, such as residents placed in jobs or connected to services. The data includes development name, borough, and multiple resident count and wage fields. Many counts are suppressed as "< 5" to protect privacy, and some fields have substantial missing values, so totals should be interpreted with care. The dataset can be used to compare economic outcomes across developments and boroughs, track trends over time, evaluate the reach and effectiveness of resident empowerment programs, and inform policy or budget decisions aimed at improving employment and financial stability for public housing residents.

name: DOHMH Childcare Center Inspections (Historical)
description:
This dataset contains historical inspection records for childcare centers regulated by the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Each row represents a violation or inspection finding tied to a specific center, identified by name, legal name, address, borough, ZIP code, phone, and permit details including permit number, expiration, and permit date. Center characteristics such as age range served, maximum capacity, program type, facility type, and childcare type are included, along with counts of educational workers.

Inspection-level fields cover the inspection date, regulation summary, violation category, health code subsection, violation status, and the overall inspection result. The data also includes computed performance metrics: violation rates, average violation rates, public health hazard violation rates, and critical violation rates, each paired with a center or citywide average for comparison. name: DOHMH Childcare Center Inspections (Historical)
description:
This dataset contains historical inspection records for childcare centers regulated by the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Each row represents a single inspection event at a licensed childcare program, with 34 columns covering facility identity, location, permit status, program and age-range characteristics, capacity, staffing, and inspection outcomes.

Key fields include the center and legal name, building, street, borough, ZIP code, and phone; permit number, permit expiration, and status (Permitted, Active, or Expired-In Renewal); program type (mostly preschool, with infant/toddler and camp programs), facility type, age range served, and maximum capacity. Inspection details include the inspection date, summary result (such as passed or reinspection required), regulation summary text, violation category (general, critical, or public health hazard), health code subsection, and violation status (corrected or open). name: DOHMH Childcare Center Inspections (Historical)
description:
This dataset contains historical inspection records for New York City childcare centers regulated by the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Each row represents a single inspection and combines facility information—center and legal name, address, borough, ZIP code, phone, permit number and status, age range served, maximum capacity, program type, facility type, and childcare type—with inspection outcomes. These outcomes include inspection date, summary result, violation rates overall and for public health hazards and critical violations, average rates for comparison, educational staffing counts, regulation summaries, violation categories and health code subsections, and whether each violation was corrected or remains open.

The data covers roughly 5,000 sampled records across all five boroughs, with Brooklyn and Queens most represented. It can be used to track inspection outcomes and violation patterns across centers, boroughs, and facility types; compare compliance by capacity, program type, or staffing levels; examine trends over time; and support research or policy analysis on childcare health and safety oversight.

name: Air Quality Testing at Saratoga Village
description:
This dataset contains air quality test results collected at Saratoga Village, with 264 sampled records and 17 columns. Each record captures a date and sample location along with up to three measurement events per visit. For each event, the data includes the time of measurement, volatile organic compound (VOC) readings in parts per million, temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, relative humidity, and any field observations noted by the tester.

The structure supports comparison of air quality conditions across different times of day and locations within the site, and allows analysis of how VOC levels relate to temperature and humidity. It could be used by environmental health researchers, property managers, or public health officials to identify patterns or potential concerns in indoor or on-site air quality, to track conditions over time, or to flag locations and times warranting further testing.

name: Air Quality Testing at Saratoga Village
description:
This dataset contains air quality readings collected at Saratoga Village over eight days in September 2018. Each row records a sample from a specific location within the building, such as a basement, main area, plaster shop, compactor room, or storage room, with up to three readings taken at different times of day. For each reading, the data includes the time, volatile organic compound (VOC) levels in parts per million, temperature in Fahrenheit, and humidity, along with free-text observations noting conditions like high temperature, poor ventilation, chemical storage, cooking odors, or lack of access to a location. VOC values are often recorded as below the detection threshold (under 0.1 ppm), and many fields have missing entries, especially the observation notes and later readings.

This dataset contains air quality testing records from Saratoga Village, covering 264 sampled rows across 17 columns. Each record includes a date and sample location, with up to three measurement events per visit. For each event, the data captures the time, volatile organic compound (VOC) concentration in parts per million, temperature in Fahrenheit, humidity, and any field observations. Sample locations include areas such as the basement, main area, plaster shop, compactor room, and storage room, and the records span eight dates in September 2018.

The data could be used to track VOC levels over time and across locations, examine relationships between VOC concentrations and temperature or humidity, identify periods or sites with elevated readings, and flag measurements that may exceed health thresholds. It could also support environmental health assessments, indoor air quality investigations, or remediation planning for the site.

name: AIR_LOT_3D
description:
This dataset contains seven records describing air lots, a type of property interest in New York City where development rights above a lot are separated from the land beneath it. Each row links an air lot to its parent property through identifiers including borough, block, lot, and BBL (borough-block-lot) numbers, and provides the air lot's own number and BBL. Records also include elevation, a model field, free-text notes, and standard audit fields recording who created and last edited each entry along with the corresponding dates. Geometry is captured through shape area and shape length values.

The data could support property research, land-use and zoning analysis, or mapping of development-rights transfers involving air lots. It may be useful to planners, appraisers, and analysts examining how air rights are structured relative to parent parcels, though with only seven sampled rows it is best suited to illustrative or reference purposes rather than broad statistical analysis.

name: AIR_LOT_3D
description:
This dataset contains seven records describing air lot subdivisions tied to a single parent tax lot in New York City (borough 3, block 4271, lot 1, BBL 3042710001). Each row represents one air lot, identified by an air lot number (9001–9008) and a corresponding air lot BBL, along with a unique object ID. The records include geometry-derived measures of area and perimeter length, a model designation of "D," and audit fields recording who created and last edited the data and when. The elevation and notes fields are entirely empty.

Because all rows share the same parent parcel, the dataset is best suited for examining how a single lot is divided into air lots and comparing their sizes and shapes. It could support mapping or spatial analysis of lot subdivisions, verification of air lot numbering and BBL assignments, or tracking of edits to the records over time. name: AIR_LOT_3D
description:
This dataset contains records of air lots, which are three-dimensional property parcels that exist above or below ground level, likely within New York City. Each row represents one air lot and links it to its underlying parent parcel through borough, block, lot, and BBL (borough-block-lot) identifiers. The sample covers a single parent parcel (borough 3, block 4271, lot 1) with seven associated air lots numbered 9001 through 9008, each with its own BBL. The data also includes a model designation, geometry measures such as shape area and shape length, and record-keeping fields showing who created and last edited each entry and when. Elevation and notes columns are present but empty in this sample.

The dataset could be used to map and analyze vertical property rights, link air lots to their underlying tax parcels, support zoning and land-use review, and maintain air lot records in a GIS or property management system.

name: Pharmaceutical and Syringe Drop-Off Locations in NYC
description: This dataset lists locations in New York City where residents can drop off pharmaceuticals and syringes for safe disposal. Each of the 339 sampled rows describes one site, including its name, type, street address, ZIP code, phone number, operating days and hours, and any notes. Records also include the borough and neighborhood name, along with geographic identifiers such as census tract, community district, council, senate, congressional and assembly districts, police precinct, DSNY zone and district, BBL, BIN, latitude, longitude, and a point geometry. The data can be used to find nearby disposal sites, map access to safe medication and sharps disposal across neighborhoods, compare availability by borough or district, and support public health or environmental planning around proper waste disposal.

name: Pharmaceutical and Syringe Drop-Off Locations in NYC
description:
This dataset lists 339 locations in New York City where residents can drop off pharmaceuticals or used syringes and sharps for safe disposal. Each row represents one site and records whether it accepts pharmaceuticals or syringes/sharps, along with the site name, street address, ZIP code, borough, and neighborhood tabulation area. Where available, it also includes phone number, operating days and hours, and notes such as whether the drop-off is in a lobby or requires calling ahead.

Each site is geocoded with latitude, longitude, and a point geometry, and is linked to administrative boundaries including community district, DSNY zone and district, census tract, city council, state senate and assembly, congressional, and police precinct districts. Building and lot identifiers (BBL and BIN) are included for most sites. name: Pharmaceutical and Syringe Drop-Off Locations in NYC
description:

Each record identifies the site by name and type (pharmaceuticals drop-off or syringe/sharps drop-off), and includes its street address, borough, ZIP code, phone number, and operating days and hours, with notes on placement or instructions where available. Records also carry neighborhood names and a range of administrative geographies—community district, census tract, council, senate, congressional, assembly, and police districts, plus sanitation zones—along with latitude and longitude coordinates and a point geometry for mapping.

The data covers all five boroughs, with Brooklyn and Queens accounting for the largest shares of sites. Phone numbers, hours, and notes are missing for roughly 40% of rows, and a small number of records lack police precinct, parcel, or building identifiers.

name: 2017 Diversity Report Admissions Methods
description: This dataset lists New York City public schools with information on their admissions methods for the 2017 diversity reporting cycle. Each row represents one school, identified by its district-borough-number code (dbn) and school name. The admissions_methods column describes how students are admitted to the school, and the fully_screened column indicates whether the school uses fully screened admissions. With roughly 1,500 school records and four fields, the data supports comparisons of admissions approaches across schools, analysis of how common screened versus other admissions methods are, and joining to other school-level datasets for research on enrollment equity and school choice.

name: 2017 Diversity Report Admissions Methods
description:

Each row represents a school, identified by its District Borough Number (dbn) and school name, with details on how students are admitted. The admissions_methods column records the specific method or methods for a school, often prefixed by school level (for example, K for kindergarten, MS for middle school, or HS for high school), such as "K: Choice District" or "MS: Limited Unscreen…". The fully_screened column indicates whether a school's admissions process is fully screened, with values like "K: No", "MS: No", or "Yes", again often tied to school level.

name: 2017 Diversity Report Admissions Methods
description:
This dataset lists New York City public schools and their admissions methods, drawn from the 2017 Diversity Report. Each row represents a school, identified by its DBN code and name, with details on the admissions method used and whether the school is fully screened. Admissions methods are labeled by school level (for example, K, MS, or HS) and include categories such as choice district and limited unscreened. The fully screened field indicates whether a school uses screened admissions, with values like "K: No" or "HS: No."

With about 1,500 rows and four columns, the data supports analysis of how selective admissions are distributed across schools and districts. It could be used to compare admissions approaches by borough or district, study the prevalence of screened versus unscreened admissions, and support research or reporting on school choice and equity in enrollment policy.

name: 2015-16 Local Law 15 Health Data - K-12 Health Instructors
description: This dataset lists New York City K-12 schools and the number of teachers assigned to teach health at each school, based on reporting under Local Law 15 for the 2015-16 school year. Each row represents one school, identified by its school DBN (District Borough Number) and name, along with its community school district and city council district. The final column gives the count of teachers assigned to health instruction at that school. With about 1,600 school records, the data can be used to compare health teaching staffing across schools, districts, and council districts; to identify schools with few or no assigned health instructors; and to support analyses of health education capacity and resource allocation in city schools.

name: 2015-16 Local Law 15 Health Data - K-12 Health Instructors
description:
This dataset lists New York City K-12 schools and the number of teachers assigned to teach health education at each school for the 2015-16 school year, reported under Local Law 15. Each row represents one school, identified by its school DBN code and name, along with its community school district and city council district. The main measure is the count of teachers assigned to teach health, which ranges from 0 to 82 per school, with a median of about 9.

The data can be used to compare health instruction staffing across schools, districts, and council districts; to identify schools with few or no assigned health teachers; and to support analyses of equity in health education resources. It could also be joined with other school-level datasets using the DBN or district fields for broader education research.

name: 2015-16 Local Law 15 Health Data - K-12 Health Instructors
description:
This dataset reports the number of teachers assigned to teach health at individual New York City public schools during the 2015-16 school year, as required under Local Law 15. Each row represents one school, identified by its school DBN (a unique school code), school name, community school district, and city council district, along with the count of health instructors assigned there. The file covers 1,627 schools across 33 community school districts and 51 city council districts, with staffing counts ranging from zero to 82 teachers per school.

The data can be used to examine how health instruction staffing is distributed across the city, compare capacity between districts or council districts, and flag schools with few or no assigned health teachers. It supports policy and budget analysis of health education resources, geographic mapping of staffing patterns, and research on whether health instruction capacity varies by district or neighborhood.

Each row represents one incident and includes when it occurred, the borough, the bus company, bus and route numbers, the run type (such as Special Ed AM Run or General Ed AM Run), and the reported reason, with heavy traffic accounting for most delays. The data can be used to analyze the frequency and causes of bus disruptions by borough, company, route, or run type; to measure delay lengths and student impact; to evaluate contractor performance and notification practices; and to inform planning or policy decisions aimed at improving school bus reliability

Each record links a person to a collision and, where applicable, a vehicle, and includes crash date and time, person type (occupant, pedestrian, bicyclist, or other motorized), injury status, age, sex, ejection, emotional status, bodily injury details, seating position, safety equipment use, pedestrian location and action, complaint, role in the crash, and up to two contributing factors. The sample covers a short window of crash dates and includes substantial missing values in several fields, particularly pedestrian-specific and contributing-factor columns.

The data can be used to study injury patterns and risk factors by person type, age, sex, or safety equipment use; to examine common contributing factors and pedestrian behaviors in crashes; to analyze crash timing; and to support traffic safety research, policy evaluation, and prevention planning.

name: Inmate Deaths
description: This dataset records reported inmate deaths in correctional facilities, with one row per incident. Each record includes an incident identifier, the date the incident was reported, the type of incident (such as death or related classification), and the facility where it occurred. With 22 sampled rows and four columns, it provides a compact log of individual incidents rather than aggregate statistics. The data could be used to track the frequency and timing of reported inmate deaths, compare incident counts across facilities, identify trends over time, or support reporting and oversight analysis. It may also serve as a starting point for research or public accountability work on deaths in custody, though the small sample size limits broader statistical conclusions.

name: Inmate Deaths

This dataset records individual inmate death incidents classified as suicides, with 22 sampled rows and four columns. Each row is identified by a unique incident_id and includes the date and time the death was reported (reported_dt), the incident type (in this sample, all entries are "Suicide"), and the facility where it occurred. Facility codes include AMKC, GRVC, OBCC, EMTC, RMSC, and MDC, though the facility field is missing for roughly 23% of rows. Reported dates span from 2015 onward.

The data could support analyses of suicide deaths in custody over time, comparisons of incident counts across facilities, and identification of reporting patterns or seasonal trends. Because the sample is small and limited to a single incident type, it is best suited for exploratory review or as a starting point for broader public safety and corrections oversight work rather than for drawing statistically robust conclusions.

The data could support corrections oversight and transparency work, such as tracking suicide incidents over time, comparing counts across facilities, or examining reporting patterns. Because the extract is small and limited to a single incident type, it is best suited for illustrative or preliminary analysis rather than broad statistical conclusions.

Because the data is organized by indicator and case type, it can be filtered to compare specific measures across case categories and time periods. It is useful for monitoring trends in child support caseloads and collections, comparing performance across case types, and supporting reporting or analysis by social services agencies, researchers, and policy analysts.

name: Recycling Diversion and Capture Rates
description:
This dataset tracks recycling performance across zones and districts over time, broken down by fiscal year and month. Each of the 2,832 rows records a location (zone and district) for a specific fiscal month and year, along with the month name. The remaining columns report performance metrics: an overall diversion rate (total recycling as a share of total waste), and capture rates for paper, mixed paper and cardboard (MGP), and a combined total that factors in leaves recycling alongside paper and MGP maximums. These rates are expressed as percentages or ratios depending on the column.

The data is suited to comparing recycling performance between districts and zones, spotting seasonal patterns across months, and tracking trends from one fiscal year to the next. Analysts could use it to identify areas with low capture or diversion rates, evaluate the effect of recycling programs over time, or build dashboards and reports for waste management planning.

name: Recycling Diversion and Capture Rates
description:

With 59 districts and 12 months per year over four years, the data covers roughly 2,800 district-month records.

Four numeric measures describe recycling outcomes. The diversion rate captures total recycling as a share of total waste, ranging from about 6% to 34%. Three capture rates measure how much of the recyclable material actually available was collected: paper capture (about 17% to 73%), metal/glass/plastic (MGP) capture (about 20% to 102%), and a combined total capture rate that includes leaves (about 18% to 76%).

name: Recycling Diversion and Capture Rates

Each row represents one district's results for a given month and year, with 59 districts grouped into seven zones such as the Bronx, Manhattan, Brooklyn North, Brooklyn South, and Queens East. The data includes a diversion rate showing the share of total waste that was recycled, plus capture rates for paper, mixed paper (MGP), and leaves, each expressed as a percentage of the maximum amount that could have been recovered. A combined capture rate covering total recycling, leaves, paper, and MGP is also provided.

The data can be used to compare recycling performance across districts and zones, track changes over time, and spot areas with low capture rates that may need outreach or program adjustments. Because it spans multiple years and every month, it supports analysis of seasonal patterns such as leaf collection, evaluation of policy or program effects, and reporting against waste diversion goals.

The data can be used to track crane-related construction activity by permit, identify the types and equipment involved in street work, and analyze patterns over time based on creation and modification dates. It may be useful for urban planning, transportation and right-of-way management, construction oversight, and research into how often and where cranes are deployed for permitted street projects.

The data could be used to map sign locations and coverage by neighborhood or district, audit signage for language accessibility and compliance, assess sign conditions and types across parks, or support maintenance and wayfinding planning for parks departments and researchers.

description:
This dataset contains polygon geometries representing tax blocks, the geographic units used to organize property records, most likely for New York City. Each of the 5,000 sampled rows describes one block boundary, identified by borough code (1–5), block number, and optional section and volume numbers used in property administration. The data also includes flags for edge-of-pavement overlap and jagged street lines, along with geometry measures (shape area and shape length) and record-keeping fields such as creator, creation date, last editor, and last edit date, though the audit fields are largely missing or concentrated on a few values.

The dataset supports property mapping and assessment, joining tax lot records to block-level geography, urban planning and land-use analysis, and spatial queries or map visualizations of block boundaries. Borough and block numbers can serve as join keys to parcel-level data, while the area and length fields allow filtering or comparison of block sizes and shapes.

description:
This dataset catalogs New York City benefit programs and social services, with one row per program record (about 97 rows sampled) and 34 fields. Each record identifies a program by name, acronym, plain-language name, program code, and unique ID, and describes its category, the government agency that runs it, the population served, and the relevant age group. Records include a program description, a brief excerpt, and a "heads up" field for caveats, plus plain-language eligibility information.

A large share of the columns covers how to apply and get help. These include summaries of the application process and separate instructions for applying online, by mail, in person, or by phone, along with call-to-action labels and URLs for online applications, PDF forms, and office locations. Additional fields list required documents and ways to get assistance in person, online, by email, by calling 311, or by calling other numbers. description:
This dataset catalogs New York City benefits, programs, services, and resources, with one row per program or service (97 rows in this sample). Each record includes a unique ID, program name and acronym, page type (Program, Service, Benefit, or Resource), category (such as cash and expenses, housing, health, work, or family services), the administering government agency, and the population and age groups served. It also provides plain-language descriptions, eligibility summaries, and "heads up" notes, along with detailed application instructions covering online, mail, in-person, and phone options, including application URLs, downloadable PDF forms, office location links, and call-to-action labels. Additional fields describe required documents, help and support channels (online, in-person, email, 311, and other phone lines), and a last-updated timestamp. Text fields contain HTML markup and are in English.

name: NYC Benefits Platform: Benefits and Programs Dataset
description:
This dataset catalogs New York City public benefits and social service programs, with each row describing a single program or service. It covers program names, acronyms, categories (such as cash and expenses, housing, health, work, and family services), administering agencies, populations served, and age groups, along with plain-language descriptions, eligibility summaries, and important caveats. It also documents how to apply through online, mail, in-person, and phone channels, including application links, downloadable forms, required documents, and ways to get help, including 311 and agency contacts. Additional fields capture page type (program, service, benefit, or resource), language, and update timestamps.

The data could support benefits navigators and caseworkers, power a searchable or multilingual benefits finder, help researchers compare programs and application pathways, and inform outreach that identifies gaps in access or coverage.

name: Historical Licenses
description:
This dataset contains historical business license records, with 5,000 sampled rows and 27 columns. Each row represents a license and includes identifiers such as license number and type, along with creation, expiration, and status dates. Business details cover business code and description, business name, and contact phone number. Location information includes building, street, secondary street, city, state, and ZIP, plus borough code, community board, council district, borough name, latitude, longitude, BIN, BBL, and 2020 census tract and neighborhood tabulation area codes.

The data can be used to analyze licensing activity over time, track license status changes, examine the geographic distribution of licensed businesses across boroughs and neighborhoods, and join with other datasets using BIN, BBL, or census geography. It may also support research on business types, local economic trends, and neighborhood-level business patterns.

name: Historical Licenses
description:
This dataset contains historical records of business and individual licenses issued in New York City, with 5,000 sampled rows and 27 columns. Each row represents a single license and includes a license number, type (Business or Individual), creation and expiration dates, current status (such as CURRENT, FAILED TO RENEW, OUT OF BUSINESS, or SURRENDERED), and the date the status was recorded. Business details include a business code and description (for example, pawnbroker, newsstand, or second-hand dealer), the business name, and an optional secondary name.

Location information covers street address, city, state, ZIP code, borough, community board, council district, and geographic coordinates (latitude, longitude, BIN, BBL, census tract, and neighborhood tabulation area). Contact phone numbers are included where available. Coverage is overwhelmingly New York State, with most records in Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens, though a small number of out-of-state addresses appear.

It includes the license number, type (Business or Individual), creation and expiration dates, current status (such as CURRENT, FAILED TO RENEW, OUT OF BUSINESS, or SURRENDERED), and the date the status was recorded. Business details include a business code and description (for example, pawnbroker, newsstand, or second hand dealer), business name, and contact phone number where available. name: Certified Asbestos Investigators
description: This dataset lists certified asbestos investigators, with 611 records and five fields: last name, first name, certification number, expiration date, and telephone number. Each row represents one certified individual, and the expiration date indicates when their certification lapses. The data could be used to look up or verify an investigator's certification status, identify certifications nearing expiration for renewal outreach, contact certified professionals, or analyze the distribution and turnover of certified investigators over time.

name: Certified Asbestos Investigators
description:
This dataset lists 611 certified asbestos investigators, with each row representing one certified individual. It includes the investigator's last name, first name, certification number, certification expiration date, and telephone number. Certification numbers range widely, and expiration dates run into 2026 and beyond. Telephone numbers are missing for about 16% of records.

The data can be used to look up or verify an investigator's certification status and expiration, to identify certifications nearing expiration for renewal outreach, or to analyze the distribution of active investigators by name, certification number, or expiration period. It may also support contact directories for licensed asbestos inspection work.

name: Certified Asbestos Investigators
description:
This dataset is a directory of 611 certified asbestos investigators, listing each person's last name, first name, certification number, certification expiration date, and telephone number. Certification numbers are numeric identifiers, expiration dates are recorded as timestamps, and phone numbers are present for most but not all records (about 16% are missing). The records appear to come from a licensing or regulatory agency that certifies professionals to inspect buildings for asbestos.

The data can be used to verify whether an investigator holds a current certification, look up contact details for licensed professionals, or build a public-facing directory. Because expiration dates are included, it also supports tracking upcoming lapses and planning renewal reminders or outreach. Regulators could use it to monitor the certified pool, identify expired credentials, or target enforcement and compliance communications, while property owners, contractors, or the public could use it to confirm a listed investigator's status before hiring.

name: RFP Summary by Agency and Fiscal Year
description: This dataset summarizes the number of requests for proposals (RFPs) released by each city agency in each fiscal year, alongside a citywide median value for comparison. Each row lists a fiscal year, an agency name, the count of RFPs that agency released during that fiscal year, and the citywide median calendar figure for that period. With 14 sampled rows and four columns, it supports comparisons of RFP activity across agencies and over time, identification of agencies with unusually high or low procurement volumes, and benchmarking of individual agencies against the citywide median. It could be useful for procurement analysts, budget and policy staff, journalists, and researchers examining government contracting trends or agency-level purchasing behavior.

name: RFP Summary by Agency and Fiscal Year
description: This dataset summarizes the number of Requests for Proposals (RFPs) released by 14 New York City agencies during fiscal year 2020. Each row represents one agency and includes its RFP count for the year, along with a citywide median calendar value of 130 days that is repeated for every record. The data covers a single fiscal year, so comparisons are limited to differences between agencies rather than trends over time. RFP counts range from 1 to 211, with a mean of about 44 per agency. The dataset could be used to compare procurement activity across agencies, identify which agencies issued the most or fewest solicitations, or provide context for analyses of city contracting and vendor opportunities. Because it contains only one year and one repeated benchmark value, it is best suited as a snapshot or as a supporting reference rather than a standalone time-series source.

name: RFP Summary by Agency and Fiscal Year
description:
This dataset summarizes Requests for Proposals (RFPs) released by New York City agencies during fiscal year 2020. Each row represents one agency and reports the number of RFPs it released that year, along with a citywide median value of 130 shown on every row for comparison. The sample contains 14 agencies, including ACS, DCA, DCAS, DFTA, and DHS, with RFP counts ranging from 1 to 211 and a mean of about 43.5 per agency.

The data can be used to compare procurement activity across agencies, highlight which agencies released unusually high or low numbers of RFPs, and benchmark individual agencies against the citywide median. It also supports transparency and oversight of government contracting, budget analysis, and reporting on public procurement trends. Because the sample covers only fiscal year 2020, its usefulness for tracking trends over time would depend on additional years of data.

name: Real-World Fuel Efficiency
description: This dataset compares real-world fuel efficiency against EPA estimates for 106 vehicle records spanning multiple model years, makes, and models. Each row identifies a vehicle by year, make, and model, and notes whether it is hybrid or non-hybrid along with its standard type. It includes EPA city fuel economy ratings alongside telematics-derived actual driving data: vehicle count, total actual miles driven, total actual fuel consumed, and EPA-expected fuel, from which actual fuel economy and the percent difference between actual and expected performance are calculated. Estimated fuel costs per unit and fuel costs per mile are also provided. The data can be used to assess how closely real-world fuel economy matches EPA ratings across vehicle types, to compare hybrid and conventional vehicles, to identify models with the largest efficiency gaps, and to estimate per-mile fuel expenses for consumers, fleet managers, or environmental analysts studying fuel consumption and emissions.

name: Real-World Fuel Efficiency
description:
This dataset compares real-world fuel efficiency against EPA estimates for vehicles from model years 2008 to 2019. Each row represents a vehicle make and model (with hybrid or non-hybrid designation and body type such as sedan, SUV, van, or pickup), along with the EPA city fuel economy rating and the number of vehicles tracked. It records total actual miles driven and total actual fuel consumed, alongside the fuel the EPA would have expected for those miles, the actual fuel economy measured by Geotab, and the percent difference between actual and expected consumption. Estimated fuel costs and cost per mile are also included, though these are stored as formatted text with dollar signs and spacing rather than plain numbers.

The data covers 106 sampled rows across 8 makes and 38 models, with Ford, Toyota, and Chevrolet most represented. name: Real-World Fuel Efficiency
description:
This dataset compares official EPA fuel economy estimates with real-world fuel use for 106 vehicle configurations spanning model years 2008 to 2019. Each row covers a specific year, make, model, hybrid or non-hybrid status, and vehicle type (sedan, SUV, van, or pickup), along with the EPA city rating and the number of vehicles represented. It also records total miles driven, total fuel actually consumed, and the fuel the EPA would have expected for those miles, from which actual fuel economy and the percent difference between actual and expected use are derived. Estimated fuel costs and cost per mile are included as formatted dollar strings.

The data supports analysis of the gap between advertised and real-world fuel efficiency, comparisons between hybrid and conventional vehicles, and operating cost estimates. It could be used by researchers studying energy use and emissions, fleet managers evaluating vehicle performance, or consumer-facing tools that help buyers understand likely fuel expenses. name: Adult Protective Services - Refer to Close by Referral Source
description: This dataset tracks Adult Protective Services referrals by referral source, showing how many cases were referred and how many were found ineligible, organized by report date and referral source type. Each row records a report date, the type of referral source (such as a specific agency or reporting channel), the total number of referrals received, and the total number deemed ineligible. With 96 sampled rows and four columns, it supports analysis of referral volumes over time, comparison of eligibility outcomes across referral sources, and identification of sources that generate high numbers of ineligible referrals. It could be useful for program monitoring, workload planning, quality improvement, and reporting on screening outcomes.

name: Adult Protective Services - Refer to Close by Referral Source
description:
This dataset summarizes Adult Protective Services (APS) referrals by referral source, tracking how many referrals were received and how many were found ineligible over time. Each row represents a combination of a reporting period (report_date, recorded as a timestamp at semi-annual intervals such as June 30 and December 31) and a referral source type, including Anonymous, Family Member/Friend/Neighbor, Marshal, Organization, Self, and one additional category. Two count fields capture the volume: total_referred (the number of referrals received from that source in that period) and total_ineligible (the number of those referrals determined not to meet eligibility criteria). The data spans 16 reporting periods and 6 source types, with counts ranging from 15 to over 19,000 referrals per row.

name: Adult Protective Services - Refer to Close by Referral Source
description:
This dataset contains Adult Protective Services referral counts for cases that were closed, organized by report date and referral source type. Each row represents a single reporting period and source category, such as Anonymous, Family Member/Friend/Neighbor, Marshal, Organization, or Self. For each combination, it records the total number of referrals received and the number of those referrals determined to be ineligible. Report dates appear at regular intervals, including mid-year and year-end snapshots, allowing for comparison across periods.

The data can be used to track referral volumes over time, identify which sources generate the most referrals, and calculate ineligibility rates by source. It supports trend analysis, workload and staffing assessments, and resource planning for protective services programs. Because the data is aggregated rather than individual-level, it is best suited to summary reporting and comparative analysis rather than case-level investigation.

name: NYPD Criminal Court Summons Incident Level Data (Year To Date)
description:
This dataset contains year-to-date incident-level records of criminal court summonses issued by the New York City Police Department. Each row represents a single summons and includes the date it was issued, the offense description, the relevant law section number and law description, and the summons category type. It also captures demographic information about the person summoned, including age group, sex, and race, along with geographic details such as jurisdiction code, borough, precinct of occurrence, and X/Y coordinates, latitude, longitude, and a geocoded location field. A unique summons key identifies each record.

The data can be used to analyze patterns in summons activity across offenses, categories, boroughs, and precincts, and to examine how summonses are distributed across demographic groups. The geographic fields support mapping and spatial analysis of where summonses occur, while the date field enables trend analysis over the year to date. It is useful for public safety research, policy evaluation, and community-level reporting on enforcement activity.

name: NYPD Criminal Court Summons Incident Level Data (Year To Date)
description:
This dataset contains incident-level records of criminal court summonses issued by the New York Police Department for the current year to date, based on a 5,000-row sample. Each row represents a single summons and includes a unique summons key and issuance date, along with the offense description, law section number, law description, and summons category type (for example, vehicle and traffic law, administrative code, or business-related violations). Records also include demographic details about the person summoned, such as age group, sex, and race, plus geographic information: jurisdiction code, borough, precinct of occurrence, map coordinates, latitude and longitude, and a geocoded point field.

The data can be used to analyze patterns in summons activity across offenses, laws, boroughs, and precincts; to map where summonses are concentrated; and to examine demographic breakdowns of those cited. name: NYPD Criminal Court Summons Incident Level Data (Year To Date)
description:
This dataset contains incident-level records of criminal court summonses issued by the New York City Police Department for the current year to date. Each row represents one summons and includes the summons date, offense description, law section number and law description, and summons category type. It also records demographic information about the person summoned, including age group, sex, and race, along with the jurisdiction code, borough, precinct of occurrence, and geographic coordinates (latitude, longitude, and a point geometry).

The data can be used to analyze patterns in summons activity across offense types, boroughs, and precincts; to map enforcement hotspots; and to examine demographic differences among people receiving summonses. It supports research, policy evaluation, transparency reporting, and journalistic analysis of public safety and criminal justice trends in New York City.

name: NYC Climate Budgeting Report: Resiliency Exposure Forecast - Outdoor Heat - Tree Canopy
description: This dataset comes from New York City's climate budgeting reporting and provides forecasted tree canopy coverage by neighborhood for use in assessing outdoor heat resiliency. Each row records a publication date, a Neighborhood Tabulation Area (NTA) name and abbreviation, a forecast year, and the percentage of that area covered by tree canopy. With roughly 1,310 rows and five columns, the data supports neighborhood-level comparisons of canopy coverage and tracking of projected changes over time. It can be used to identify areas with low tree cover and potentially higher heat exposure, prioritize tree planting or resiliency investments, and combine with other climate, health, or demographic data for equity and urban planning analysis.

name: NYC Climate Budgeting Report: Resiliency Exposure Forecast - Outdoor Heat - Tree Canopy
description:
This dataset contains neighborhood-level tree canopy coverage projections for New York City, published as part of the NYC Climate Budgeting Report's resiliency exposure forecast for outdoor heat. Each row pairs a neighborhood (identified by its NTA name and abbreviation) with a forecast year and the estimated percentage of that area covered by tree canopy. The data covers 262 neighborhoods across five time points (2021, 2030, 2040, 2050, and 2055), with canopy coverage ranging from under 1% to about 83% and averaging roughly 27%. All records share a single publication date of May 13, 2026.

The dataset can be used to compare tree canopy coverage across neighborhoods and to track how coverage is projected to change over time, supporting analysis of heat exposure, urban greening priorities, and equity in climate resilience planning. It is useful for planners, researchers, and advocates examining which areas have low canopy and may face greater outdoor heat risk, and for evaluating

name: NYC Climate Budgeting Report: Resiliency Exposure Forecast - Outdoor Heat - Tree Canopy
description:
This dataset contains neighborhood-level tree canopy coverage percentages for New York City, published as part of the city's climate budgeting reporting on outdoor heat exposure and resiliency. Each row represents one neighborhood tabulation area (NTA) in a given year, identified by its full name and abbreviation, along with the percentage of ground covered by tree canopy. The data covers five time points (2021, 2030, 2040, 2050, and 2055), spanning 262 distinct neighborhoods, with all records sharing a single publication date of May 13, 2026. Canopy coverage values range from under 1% to about 83%, with a typical neighborhood around 27%.

The dataset can be used to map tree canopy coverage across neighborhoods, flag areas with sparse tree cover that may face greater outdoor heat exposure, compare projected conditions across future years, and support equitable tree-planting, climate adaptation, and public health planning.

name: Research Permits
description: This dataset lists research permits issued for projects conducted in parks, with 65 sampled records and seven fields. Each row identifies the permit year, project title, and the institution conducting the research, along with the borough and park name where the work took place. It also records the specific location within the park and the taxa or subject area being studied. The data can be used to explore which institutions are active in park research, how research activity varies by year, borough, or park, and which organisms or topics attract the most study. It may be useful for park managers, researchers, educators, and anyone interested in the scope and distribution of scientific work happening in these green spaces.

name: Research Permits
description:
This dataset lists research permits granted for studies conducted in New York City parks, with 65 sampled records and seven fields. Each row captures a single permitted project, including the permit year (almost all from 2017, with a few spanning 2013–2018), the project title, the requesting institution (such as AKRF Inc. or the American Museum of Natural History), the borough, the specific park, and an optional note on the location within the park. A final field records the taxa or area of study, such as plants, mammals, birds, water quality/hydrology, or other topics.

The data can be used to examine which institutions conduct research in city parks, how research activity is distributed across boroughs and parks, and what kinds of subjects are studied. It supports mapping or summarizing research activity by geography and topic, identifying frequently studied parks, and exploring institutional participation in park research. name: Research Permits
description: This dataset lists research permits issued for projects conducted in public parks, with 65 sampled records and seven fields. Each record includes the permit year, project title, sponsoring institution, borough, park name, an optional location within the park, and the taxa or subject area of study (such as plants, mammals, birds, or water quality). Most permits are from 2017, with a small number covering a multi-year span. Boroughs include Manhattan, Queens, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Staten Island, and institutions range from universities and museums to environmental consulting firms. The data can be used to track research activity in parks over time, compare which institutions and parks host the most studies, examine how research topics are distributed across taxa and disciplines, and support planning and transparency around scientific work in public green spaces.

name: TAX_LOT_POLYGON
description:
This dataset contains polygon records for tax lots, the basic land parcels used for property assessment and billing. Each row represents one lot and includes its borough, block, and lot identifiers along with the combined borough-block-lot (BBL) number. The 22 columns also capture lot characteristics and status flags, such as whether the lot is a condominium, has a real estate tax exemption or abatement (REUC), is an air lot, sub-lot, or easement, and whether it is flagged for building or billing purposes. Additional fields record the effective tax year, free-text lot notes, creation and last-edit metadata, and geometry measures (shape area and shape length).

name: TAX_LOT_POLYGON
description:
This dataset contains tax lot polygon records, representing individual property parcels identified by borough, block, and lot numbers. Each row corresponds to one tax lot, with a unique object ID and a combined borough-block-lot (BBL) identifier. The data includes administrative and status flags such as condo, REUC, air lot, sub-lot, and easement indicators, along with notes, effective tax year, and several coded flags related to billing, building mapping, conversion exceptions, and value reflection. It also records creation and last-edit metadata (user and date) and geometric attributes including shape area and shape length. Borough codes range from 1 to 5, with the largest share of records in borough 1.

The dataset could be used for property and land-use analysis, mapping and GIS work, tax assessment research, and tracking changes to parcel records over time. name: TAX_LOT_POLYGON
description:
This dataset contains tax lot polygons for New York City, where each row represents a parcel of land identified by borough, block, lot, and a unique BBL (borough-block-lot) identifier. It includes flags for lot characteristics such as condominium status, real estate utility company status, air lots, sub-lots, and easements, along with occasional notes, effective tax year, and geometry measures including area and perimeter length. The data also records creation and last-edit metadata such as user and date.

The dataset supports property mapping and GIS analysis, identifying condominium, easement, and other special parcel types, and linking tax lots to other city datasets through the BBL identifier. It can also be used to track parcel boundary changes over time and to support urban planning, land records management, and assessment-related work.

name: Tax Credits By Agi Range
description: This dataset summarizes Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) totals broken out by income group. It has 8 rows and three columns: income_group, which identifies the adjusted gross income (AGI) bracket; total_eitc_dollars_in_millions, the total EITC amount claimed within that bracket, in millions of dollars; and number_of_eitc_recipients, the count of people receiving the credit in that bracket. Each row pairs one income range with its aggregate credit dollars and recipient count, making it possible to compare how EITC benefits are distributed across income levels. The data could be used to analyze the concentration of EITC dollars and recipients by income range, calculate average credit amounts per recipient, build charts or tables for policy or research reports, or support discussions of tax policy and low-income assistance programs.

name: Tax Credits By Agi Range
description: This dataset summarizes Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) amounts and recipient counts broken out by income decile. It contains eight rows, one for each income group from the 1st Decile through the 8th Decile, with three columns: the income group label, the total EITC dollars in millions, and the number of EITC recipients. Values range from 0 to 27.4 million dollars in credits and from 0 to about 216,000 recipients per group. The data can be used to compare how EITC dollars and recipient counts are distributed across income levels, to identify which income groups receive the most support, and to build simple charts or tables showing the relationship between income bracket and credit totals.

name: Tax Credits By Agi Range
description:
This dataset summarizes Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) activity across eight income groups, labeled by decile from the 1st Decile through the 8th Decile. For each income group it reports two measures: the total EITC dollars claimed, expressed in millions, and the number of EITC recipients. The table is small, with one row per income group and no missing values.

The data can be used to examine how EITC benefits are distributed across the income spectrum, for example by comparing dollar amounts with recipient counts to see where credit amounts are largest relative to the number of people receiving them. It supports analysis, reporting, and research on tax credit policy and low-income assistance programs, and could serve as a compact reference table or input for simple charts and comparisons.

name: BIC Complaints Inquiries
description:
This dataset contains records of complaints and inquiries filed against businesses licensed by the city, with 5,000 sampled rows and 42 columns. Each record includes a complaint or inquiry number, the date it was filed, the type of license and industry involved, the business account name and BIC number, and the account's status. It also captures how the complaint or inquiry was received, its nature and disposition, its current status, and the total response time.

Location details are provided for both the complaint location (street, city, state, zip, borough) and the business address, along with geographic identifiers such as latitude, longitude, community board, council district, census tract, BIN, BBL, and NTA. For complaints involving vehicles, the data includes vehicle make, model, type, year, and color. Additional fields indicate whether the complainant was contacted, whether contact was unsuccessful, and the method used to make contact.

name: BIC Complaints Inquiries
description:
This dataset contains records of complaints and inquiries filed against trade waste businesses, likely in New York City, with 5,000 sampled rows and 42 columns. Each record captures a complaint or inquiry number, the date it was filed, its source (such as 311 phone lines, direct phone calls, web-mail, or mail), the nature of the issue (for example billing, contracts, service, or misinformation), and how it was resolved. This dataset contains records of complaints and inquiries filed against licensed businesses, primarily trade waste and transfer station operators in New York City. Each row represents a single complaint or inquiry, identified by a unique number, and includes the date it was filed, how it was submitted (such as 311, phone, web, or mail), its nature, disposition, status, and the time taken to respond. Records also capture whether the matter was a complaint or an inquiry, whether the complainant was contacted, and the method used to reach them.

Business details include the account name, BIC license number, license type, account status, and business address and phone. Complainant location information covers street, city, state, ZIP, borough, and, where available, geographic identifiers such as latitude and longitude, community board, council district, census tract, BIN, and BBL. A small subset of records includes vehicle details such as make, model, type, year, and color.

name: Environmentally Preferable Purchasing FY15 - Construction
description: This dataset lists construction-related contracts registered by city agencies during fiscal year 2015 that fall under Environmentally Preferable Purchasing (EPP) guidelines. Each row records the agency, a description of the contract, its registration date, the EPP product type or types involved, whether the products meet EPP minimum standards (yes/no), and the contract value. With 30 sampled rows and six columns, it offers a snapshot of which agencies bought environmentally preferable construction goods, what was purchased, and how much was spent. It can be used to track compliance with EPP standards, compare spending across agencies or product types, identify contracts that fail to meet minimum standards, and support reporting or analysis of sustainable procurement practices in city government.

name: Environmentally Preferable Purchasing FY15 - Construction
description:

description:

Each row represents a proposed residential development project and includes the property address, borough, tax block and lot, building identification number, permit sequence, and geographic identifiers such as latitude, longitude, community board, council district, census tract, and neighborhood tabulation area. Records also capture project details including total reported units, restricted affordable units, affordability option selected, commencement and anticipated dates, and submission date. name: The relationship between domestic violence and shooting incidents in New York City
description: This dataset examines the relationship between domestic violence and shooting incidents across New York City police precincts. Each row represents a precinct or location type and includes counts of shootings and overall domestic violence incidents, along with precinct population figures and corresponding rates per population. The data also breaks down actual versus expected shooting and domestic violence counts by race and ethnicity (white, black, Asian/Pacific Islander, American Indian, and other) and by sex (male and female), alongside citywide population figures for each group. With 83 sampled rows and 43 columns, the dataset supports analysis of how domestic violence levels relate to gun violence geographically, and whether shootings and domestic violence incidents are distributed across demographic groups in proportion to their share of the population. It could be useful for public safety researchers, policy analysts, and community organizations studying crime patterns, resource allocation, or disparities in policing outcomes.

description:

Each row represents a geographic area—most often a police precinct, with a few rows covering boroughs or the city as a whole—and reports counts of shootings and domestic violence incidents alongside population figures and derived rates.

The core measures include total shootings, overall domestic violence incidents, population, and per-population rates for both shootings and domestic violence. These allow comparison of incident frequency relative to area population size. The dataset also includes a set of citywide breakdowns by race/ethnicity and by sex, comparing actual counts of shootings and domestic violence incidents against expected counts based on population shares. Each row represents a precinct (with a few borough- and city-level summary rows), and includes total shootings, total domestic violence incidents, population, and calculated rates per population for both measures. The data also includes breakdowns of actual versus expected shooting and domestic violence counts by race and by sex, along with corresponding New York City population figures used to derive those expectations.

With 83 rows and 43 columns, the dataset supports analyses of whether precincts with higher domestic violence rates also experience more shootings, comparisons of observed incident counts against demographically expected counts to examine disparities, and geographic comparisons across precincts. It could be used by researchers, policymakers, or analysts studying the overlap between domestic violence and gun violence, allocating public safety resources, or investigating demographic patterns in violent incidents. Note that many of the race- and sex-breakdown columns are populated in only one row

name: Rates of Intimate Partner Violence Across New York City: An Intersectional Analysis
description: This dataset provides counts of intimate partner violence (assault) incidents and population figures across New York City geographic locations, broken down by race/ethnicity and sex. Each row represents a geographic area and includes population counts for five racial/ethnic groups (white, black, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, and American Indian) overall and separately for females and males, alongside corresponding assault counts for each group and sex. The dataset also includes expected assault counts by race/ethnicity, which can be compared with observed counts to identify disparities. With 61 rows and 36 columns, it supports intersectional analysis of how intimate partner violence rates vary across race, gender, and neighborhood, and could be used for public health research, resource allocation, policy evaluation, and identifying communities with elevated risk or underreporting.

description:

Each of the 61 rows represents a geographic location—the citywide total plus individual areas such as the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, and Queens—with 36 columns covering population size, observed assault counts, and expected assault counts for White, Black, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, and American Indian groups, each further split into female and male categories.

name: Rates of Intimate Partner Violence Across New York City: An Intersectional Analysis
description:
This dataset contains counts of intimate partner violence assaults across 61 New York City geographic locations, broken down by race, ethnicity, and sex. Each row represents a location and includes population counts for five racial and ethnic groups (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, and American Indian), further split by female and male. Alongside these population figures, the data records observed assault counts for each group and sex, as well as expected assault counts by racial and ethnic group. The locations range from the citywide total to individual boroughs and smaller neighborhoods.

The data supports intersectional analysis of disparities in intimate partner violence, allowing comparisons of observed versus expected assault counts to identify groups and areas where violence is higher or lower than population-based expectations. It could be used by researchers, public health analysts, and policymakers to study patterns of violence across race, ethnicity, and sex, to compare boroughs and neighborhoods, and to guide the targeting of prevention and support resources toward disproportionately affected communities.

name: Natural Turf Maintenance
description: This dataset contains records of natural turf maintenance work carried out at parks and open spaces, with 5,000 sampled rows and 14 columns. Each row describes a single work visit, including the date of work, borough and district, site name and property ID, start and end times, and crew size. It also records whether the crew completed mowing, trimming, and blowing tasks, whether all assigned tasks were completed, and a reason when they were not. The data can be used to track maintenance activity and crew performance across sites and districts, identify patterns in incomplete work, compare response times for different task types, and support planning or reporting on groundskeeping operations.

name: Natural Turf Maintenance
description:
This dataset records daily natural turf maintenance work assignments for parks and green spaces across New York City's five boroughs, sampled at 5,000 rows. Each record represents a work order identified by a unique ID and linked to a specific site, property ID, borough, and maintenance district. Records include the date of work, scheduled start and end times, and crew size, along with whether mowing, trimming, and blowing tasks were performed. Response fields distinguish completed work from tasks that were not needed, including cases skipped due to drought conditions. A completion flag indicates whether the crew finished all assigned tasks, and a reason field (populated mainly for incomplete work) captures causes such as end of day, staffing, equipment issues, or site in use.

name: Natural Turf Maintenance
description:
This dataset records natural turf maintenance work performed at parks and public green spaces, organized by borough, district, and site name. Each row represents a work assignment on a given date, with start and end times, crew size, and whether mowing, trimming, and blowing tasks were completed. It also flags whether the crew was able to complete assigned tasks and, when not, the reason (for example, end of day, staffing, equipment, or site in use). The sample covers 5,000 rows across 14 columns, with sites concentrated in Queens, the Bronx, Staten Island, Brooklyn, and Manhattan.

The data can be used to analyze crew productivity and task completion rates, identify sites or districts with frequent incomplete work and the reasons behind it, examine geographic or seasonal patterns in maintenance activity, and support resource planning and service-level reporting for park upkeep.

name: 2016-17 Physical Education - PE Space
description: This dataset lists physical education spaces used by schools for the 2016-17 school year, with 5,000 sampled rows and 16 columns. Each row describes a single PE space, including its location by borough, geographical district, and administrative district, along with an ATS code, location name, and building ID and name. It records the grade level served, ownership status, room number, square footage, room function, whether the space is shared with other schools, whether it is inside or outside, and whether it is used for any purpose besides PE. A location field provides geographic coordinates. The data could be used to analyze the supply and size of PE facilities across districts and boroughs, compare indoor and outdoor spaces, identify shared or multi-use facilities, and examine how space availability relates to grade levels or school characteristics.

name: 2016-17 Physical Education - PE Space
description:
This dataset lists physical education spaces in New York City public school buildings for the 2016-17 school year. Each row describes one room or outdoor area tied to a specific school, identified by its ATS code and location name, along with the building it occupies. Records include the borough, geographic and administrative district, grade level served (elementary through high school), building ownership type, room number, square footage, and the room's function, such as gymnasium, outdoor yard, multi-purpose classroom, dance room, or weight room. Flags indicate whether the space is indoors or outdoors, whether it is shared with other schools, and whether it is used for purposes other than physical education.

The data can support analyses of PE facility capacity and equity across boroughs and districts, comparisons of indoor versus outdoor space, and identification of schools that share or repurpose their PE areas. It is useful for school administrators, urban planners, and researchers studying how physical activity resources are distributed across the school system.

name: 2016-17 Physical Education - PE Space
description: This dataset lists physical education spaces in New York City public schools for the 2016-17 school year. Each row describes one room or facility, identified by school code, location name, building ID, and building name, along with its borough, geographic and administrative district, and grade level served. Rows also record ownership type, room number, square footage, room function (such as gymnasium, outdoor yard, multi-purpose classroom, dance room, or weight room), whether the space is shared with other schools, whether it is indoors or outdoors, and whether it is used for any purpose besides PE. The data can be used to compare the availability and size of PE facilities across boroughs and districts, examine differences in space allocation between school types, assess how often PE spaces are shared or repurposed, and support facilities planning and investment decisions.

name: Lottery Applications for Tobacco Retail Dealer (TRD) and Electronic Cigarette Dealer Licenses (ECD)
description: This dataset lists lottery applications submitted for Tobacco Retail Dealer (TRD) and Electronic Cigarette Dealer (ECD) licenses. Each row represents one applicant and includes the applicant name, application submission date, lottery order and priority numbers, lottery selection date, whether the applicant was selected from the lottery, and the resulting license application number. Location details cover city, state, ZIP code, borough, and community district, along with record identifiers and category/sub-type fields that distinguish the license type. With 26 sampled rows and 16 columns, the data can be used to examine lottery outcomes and selection patterns, compare application volumes across boroughs and community districts, track timelines from submission to selection, and support research or reporting on local tobacco and e-cigarette retail licensing.

name: Lottery Applications for Tobacco Retail Dealer (TRD) and Electronic Cigarette Dealer Licenses (ECD)
description:
This dataset lists lottery applications submitted for Tobacco Retail Dealer (TRD) licenses in New York, with each row representing one applicant and their application details. The sample covers 26 applications, all submitted in 2022, and includes the applicant's name, submission date, lottery order and priority numbers, selection date, and whether the applicant was selected in the lottery. It also records location information such as city, borough, ZIP code, and community district, plus a license application number where one has been assigned (missing for about 42% of rows).

The data could be used to examine the geographic distribution of tobacco retail license applicants across Brooklyn, the Bronx, and Manhattan, to study lottery outcomes and priority rankings, or to track the progression from lottery selection to formal license application. It may also be useful for research on retail licensing patterns in specific neighborhoods or for transparency reporting on how licenses are allocated.

name: Lottery Applications for Tobacco Retail Dealer (TRD) and Electronic Cigarette Dealer Licenses (ECD)
description:
This dataset contains records of lottery applications for Tobacco Retail Dealer and Electronic Cigarette Dealer licenses, with each row representing one applicant. Fields include the applicant's name, application submission date, lottery order and priority number, lottery selection date, whether the applicant was selected, and the resulting license application number where one exists. Location details cover city, state, ZIP code, borough, and community district, all within New York. The sample is limited to Tobacco Retail Dealer applications submitted in 2022, concentrated in Brooklyn and the Bronx.

The data can be used to examine how the lottery selection process played out for applicants, compare submission timing with selection outcomes, and map where applicants are located across boroughs and community districts. It also supports analysis of demand for tobacco and e-cigarette retail licenses and transparency or policy research on retail licensing.

name: MISC_TEXT
description: This dataset contains 3,018 sampled records from a City Government source, organized into two columns: misc_text and rotation. The misc_text column holds free-form text entries, while the rotation column records an associated rotation value for each entry. The data appears to capture miscellaneous text items paired with a rotation indicator, though the exact meaning of the rotation field is not specified. With roughly 3,000 rows, it offers a modest sample suitable for exploring text patterns, grouping or filtering entries by rotation value, or as a reference list for city-related records. It could support tasks such as text categorization, quality checks on free-form entries, or joining with other city datasets that share the rotation identifier.

name: MISC_TEXT
description:

The misc_text column holds 2,143 distinct free-form entries such as street names (LOCUST AVE), identifiers (P2776, C2205-18A), and numeric codes (499-C, 450-C), with about 0.1% of values missing. The rotation column is a float measuring an angle in degrees, ranging from 0 to just under 360, with a mean near 144 degrees and about 10% of values missing.

Because the text values are heterogeneous and lack a defined schema, the dataset is best suited for exploratory work: cataloging and standardizing label or identifier formats, linking entries to other city records, or analyzing the distribution of rotation angles. name: MISC_TEXT
description:
This dataset contains about 3,000 rows of short free-text entries from a city government context, each paired with a numeric rotation value. The text column holds 2,143 distinct values, mostly brief codes, labels, and street or location references such as "LOCUST AVE," "P2776," and "450-C," with a small share of missing entries. The rotation column is a float ranging from 0 to about 360, with a mean near 144 and roughly 10% of values missing, suggesting an angle or ordering measure used to cycle or position items.

The data could be used to catalog and deduplicate municipal text entries, train or test text classification and normalization workflows, or manage the display order of messages and labels via the rotation field. It may also serve as a reference list for matching short codes and location names in other city records.

name: Raised Crosswalk Locations
description: This dataset lists raised crosswalk locations, with 159 records and six fields. Each record identifies a treatment type, a date, a node ID, and the crosswalk's geometry in WKT format along with its x and y coordinates. The data can be used to map and inventory raised crosswalks, compare treatment types, track when locations were recorded, and support transportation planning, safety analysis, or GIS mapping of pedestrian infrastructure.

name: Raised Crosswalk Locations
description: This dataset lists raised crosswalk locations, with 159 sampled records and six columns. Each row represents a single raised crosswalk treatment, identified by a treatment type, a date, a node ID, and point geometry. The treatment column is mostly "Raised Crosswalk" (about 89%), with smaller shares for variants such as raised crosswalks on specific intersection legs, mid-block raised crosswalks, and other leg-specific labels. The date field records when each entry was logged or installed, spanning multiple years. The nodeid column gives a numeric network node reference for most records, and wkt_geometry stores each location as a point in well-known text format.
